english.fix: A short drive from the high-rise apartments of Chungbuk Innovation City brings you into an entirely different landscape. At the end of a lane barely wide enough for one car, where an old mission station and a cross are the first to greet visitors at the village entrance, you have arrived at Bongam Shrine in Eumseong. This is where Bangchukgol and Gyemadae, two Catholic villages whose believers settled after the Gihae Persecution of 1839, once stood; Father Choe Yang-eop stopped here to give the sacraments and chose a seminarian, and six believers bore witness with their blood. The Diocese of Cheongju proclaimed it a shrine on November 29, 2020. Today we will begin at the Bongam station, then follow the history of the two villages, Father Choe's visit, the martyrdoms of the Byeongin Persecution, and the story of a shrine being built as believers donate land one pyeong at a time.

The Bongam station is a place that has kept the root of faith since 1897. After the Byeongin Persecution destroyed the Catholic villages, Joseph Jeong Mu-seon moved to Bongam in 1892 and rebuilt a community of faith, and this station, founded in 1897, has kept that root alive ever since. On November 29, 2020, Bishop Jang Bong-hun of Cheongju proclaimed it a shrine in order to remember the place Father Thomas Choe Yang-eop, the 'martyr of sweat,' visited, where a seminary candidate was chosen, and where the forebears of Bangchukgol and Gyemadae preserved their faith through persecution. Eumseong County has a Catholic population of about fifteen percent, the highest in the Diocese of Cheongju, and three stations, Maengdong, Yupo, and Bongam, lie within four kilometers, a sign of how long the faith has been rooted here.

Since the proclamation, Father Jeong Gwang-yeol, pastor of Maengdong parish and in charge of the shrine, and the parishioners have pooled their efforts to build it. The 'one pyeong of land for Bongam Shrine' campaign begun in the second half of 2019 had passed 540 pyeong by the spring of 2021, and the station's own 190 pyeong plus 540 pyeong nearby have been purchased. The Gyemadae land has been promised as a gift, while the Bangchukgol land has not yet been secured. Around a shrine that had nothing, the small contributions of the faithful have created a rose garden and a line of roadside trees, and Eumseong County has agreed to widen the access road. Father Jeong, who is always in work clothes clearing paths and cutting trees whenever there is no Mass, is called 'the ox priest' in the village, and the parishioners too, without being asked, haul away discarded wood and tend the flower beds, building the shrine together.

This concludes our visit to Bongam Shrine in Eumseong, a place for experiencing where the forebears kept their faith through hardship, and one waiting to grow into a spiritual refuge for the region. Baeti Shrine in Jincheon, where John Kim studied, and the martyrdom site in Chungju where Min Yun-myeong died are also worth visiting together.
